utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before we call our next witness, there are just two small procedural matters to resolve with respect to the witness, and it requires us to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, in September of 1991, could you tell us approximately how many people lived in Nadin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you say approximately how many houses there were in Nadin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 150 or maybe 120.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was Nadin a Croatian village, a Serbian village, or was it mixed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two Serb houses; the rest were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How far is Nadin from Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In September of 1991, did you have running water and electricity in Nadin, was it working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why not? What had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were switched off in August. From Benkovac they switched off our electricity and we did not have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who's "they"? Who switched it off, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbs there, the Orthodox Serbs, the local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In September of 1991, can you tell us to your knowledge approximately how many weapons existed in Nadin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, only hunting rifles. There were maybe five or six hunters in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers or armed units or fighters located in Nadin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: To your knowledge in September of 1991, did the village of Nadin pose any threat to any Serbs living in areas around Nadin, for example in Benkovac or other areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On the 18th of September, 1991, what happened in Nadin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shells were falling, and then women and children were taken out and driven to the village of Polaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there any warning before the shells started falling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell what direction the shells came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, either from Biljani or Lisan. Those were neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were those villages under Serb control or Croat control or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under Serb control.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that when the shells started falling that the women and children were taken out. Who took them out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People. Everybody looked after their own and took them away to Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why did they take them away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were afraid. Other villages had already fallen, and the children and women there had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember what other villages had already fallen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lisani, some villages around Benkovac, Polaca, Krusevo, a number of the villages in Bukovica around Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After the shelling started on the 18th of September, 1991, was there any more shelling in September or October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 2nd of October there was another round of shelling. They had already entered Nadin, and two lads got killed. I forgot to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, these are just going to be general questions, so please do not mention your name or the names of other people. On the 18th of November, 1991, in the morning did something happen in Nadin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shells started falling around 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell me approximately how many people remained in the village at that time -- were in the village at that time on the 18th of November. You told us before that there were about 300 people who lived there. How many people remained at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only males and a few women who prepared food for them -- actually, the women and the children were the first to leave, and I don't know how many people remained in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On that day, on the 18th of November, 1991, were there any Croatian soldiers or military units or military forces of any kind in Nadin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You told us before that in September of 1991 there were about -- that there were only hunting weapons and that there were about five hunters in Nadin. In November of 1991, was there any change or was it the same? Were there any other weapons at that time or was it the same as before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same. The situation was the same. Nothing changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On that day, on the 18th of November, 1991, did the villagers of Nadin pose a threat to Serbs anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, when you returned to Nadin after Operation Storm, can you tell the Trial Chamber what you saw.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I saw a terrible sight. All the houses had been burnt, the trees, the forest, everything was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell if anything had been taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, you could see that some things had been taken, the tractor, the characters, some newer furniture from the house, the appliances. Everything that was new was taken away, if -- the older things were left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, was there a church in Nadin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the condition of the church when you returned after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The church had also been destroyed and burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What kind of a church was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How do you mean what kind?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was it a Catholic church or an Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, a Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, those are all my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would that then be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has no questions for this witness, and in -- I would like the Trial Chamber to bear that in mind in view of the connections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for mentioning that, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, this brings us to the end of your testimony. We thank you very much for coming to testify, and I just want to say on behalf of the Tribunal that we really appreciate you -- the effort you've put in to coming to testify, notwithstanding -- are we in -- we are in public session? Can we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Then I can say I don't know why Mr. Whiting always takes the word out of my mouth. Be that as it may, I thank you very much. I think it is also for the Chamber to endorse what Mr. Whiting has said and express its gratitude and appreciation to the technicians and the people in the field for mounting up the videolink at such a short notice. And we understand we have put them into some inconvenience, and we hope it will not recur, but we appreciate the stellar job that you did. Thank you so much. I wanted us to finish the business for the day, and then we can adjourn for good for the weekend. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, bearing in mind what you just said, I wanted to make a request of the Trial Chamber. May we go back into private session for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do we still have sufficient recording space on our tapes now that it looks like -- I'm not quite sure whether we can stay longer. Or should we take a short break, even if it's a 15-minute one, and come back at 4.00? I see a -- there's a nod and -- there's a nod in agreement this side and there's a disagreement this side, if I look at the booths. I'm not sure who to go with. Mr. Milovancevic, maybe you must be the arbiter here. If we gave you a 15-minute break and then come back just to finalise this, would that be okay? I think we'll do that. Let's come back at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I see you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if you wanted me to address the points with regard to the Defence filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a few points to make, Your Honour. The first is a procedural point, which I don't -- I won't insist on but I will raise, which is that in our view -- in our submission, we should have been provided with the full filing, not a redacted filing. There is a paragraph which was filed ex parte, paragraph 14, which appears to be -- concern remuneration to the Defence. I understand that normally that is an issue which is between the Defence and the Registry and the Trial Chamber, and it's not something that we have any interest in and any concern about. However, when that issue starts to have an impact on the trial schedule and is raised in a submission to the Trial Chamber to change the trial schedule that has been set, then I think the matter changes, and it becomes something that we do have an interest in and should be included in. So I do think that that is something that we should have been provided. But as I said, it's not something that I'm going to press any further than that, just to raise that point. The second point, Your Honour, is that we are prepared to stay with the schedule that has been ordered by the Trial Chamber in its Scheduling Order, and we do think that it is important to keep the schedule on -- keep the trial on track and to complete the trial as expeditiously as possible for the sake of all the parties, for the accused, and for everybody. I'm not going to address the points raised by the Defence. I will defer to the Trial Chamber on those points to consider and weigh those. We would be concerned about any change in the schedule that would reduce the time that the Prosecution has between the time that we get the list of witnesses from the Defence and the time the first Defence witness is called. As the schedule now stands, that is a period of 12 days. We would be very concerned and would even oppose any change in the schedule which further reduces that time of 12 days. For -- to us, that's the minimum amount of time. We're prepared to do it in 12 days, but we would not want it to be less than 12 days. So when we look at the various options, it seems to us that there are, in a way, two different approaches. One is to stick with the schedule as we have it now; the second approach would essentially to be -- would essentially be to give up the aspiration to have the Defence case -- Defence witnesses start before the break and to simply accomplish all the other business between now and the break, which is the 98 bis submission, the decision on the 98 bis, and the Defence filings. It seems to us that if the Trial Chamber wants to have the Defence witnesses start on the 10th of July of this year, then we have to stick to the schedule that has been proposed by the Court. There's no other way really to adjust it without impinging on the Trial Chamber's time to consider the 98 bis arguments and the Prosecution's time to prepare for the Defence case. So option one is -- we think is to stay with the schedule as it stands now; option two is to essentially plan for the Defence witnesses to start after the break and then to schedule back, as it were, from that date and to accomplish the 98 bis submissions, the 98 bis decision, and the filing of the 65 ter (G) documents, the Defence witness list and exhibit list, all before the break occurs in July. The only final matter I would raise is that if possible -- if it's possible, current -- under the current schedule, the date of the 23rd -- Friday, the 23rd of June, a week from today, is now free. If at all possible, I don't know if the Trial Chamber is planning on changing the dates at all, but if that could remain free, I would be most grateful. I've now scheduled something for that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 23rd of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: 23rd of June, that's a week from today, which under the current schedule the Trial Chamber is free. We're not sitting on that day for any purpose. So if it's possible to keep that date free, I would be grateful because I've scheduled something else for that date. Unless the Trial Chamber has any questions, those are really our submissions. And I guess finally I would say again that we would seek resolution of this matter today and that all the dates be decided so that we know and can plan accordingly, that all the dates between now and the beginning of the Defence case be decided and finally resolved once -- you know, for good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I'm sorry to -- I had to confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As far as the issues are concerned raised by the Prosecutor, we have a decision, the decision on schedule exists at the moment. The Defence has filed a motion that the Trial Chamber is going to consider. The Prosecutor insists on the Trial Chamber breaking the 65 ter (G) rule and to rule on the schedule without the Prosecutor completing their case. This is done only after the completion of the Prosecution case. The Prosecutor is today in a haste, although neither the Defence nor the Trial Chamber have led to this delay. This is the matter of the procedure and it's up to the Prosecutor. I have stated my reasons for which I have asked for our work to be shorter today. I have nothing to add to that reason, and I believe it would only be polite and courteous if my learned friend has taken my reason into account. Thank you very much. As for all the issues that have been raised in our submission and the issues that have been raised by my learned friend from the Prosecution, we can discuss those on Monday morning. And as for the schedule that is -- that exists is something binding upon us as well as upon my learned friend, until the Trial Chamber decides differently. In order for the Trial Chamber to decide differently, our voice has to be heard, and I have explained why I am ill-disposed to say anything today, and I would kindly ask all concerned to bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. The Bench has certainly heard what you have to say. And in consideration of that point and the points raised by the Prosecution, the Bench is going to make the following ruling at the moment: That the Bench wants to consider the submissions of the parties further before it makes any decision, barring the fact that the decision that is going to be made -- I beg your pardon. Not the decision that is going to be made. Barring the fact that the Prosecution case must still close on the 20th of June. Okay. And then the rest of the other issues we'll deal with on Monday, and we are going to try to accommodate everyone as far as is possible. Some people may not be absolutely accommodated, and you've got to bear in mind that the Chamber is also very much inclined to start with the Defence case before we go on recess. That is also an important point on the side of the Bench to consider for various other reasons that -- some of which I'm sure you are aware of. In short, the ruling then is that we are going to adjourn, we are going to consider the matter, but the Defence -- the Prosecution must finish its Prosecution case by the 20th of June. Okay. That brings us to the close of that matter. Mr. Milovancevic, having said that, I'm not quite sure how urgent it is for me to give a decision on protective measures for a Prosecution witness. I know that we're getting close, and I don't know how -- Witness 45, can we do that on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We can, Your Honour. I actually anticipate that that witness may not end up testifying. At the moment he's refusing to testify, so we certainly do not need to deal with it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Court adjourned. Reconvened on Monday - what is the date on Monday? - the 19th, at 9.00 in the morning in this courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 19th day of June, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.15 p.m.,
